name: Arba
title: The greatest man among the Anakim
summary:
Arba is regarded as the ancestor of the Anakites, a feared people of giants in the Canaanite highlands.  
He is described as the greatest among them (Josh 14:15), and the city Kiriath-Arba – 'Arba's city' – was named after him.  
This city later became known as Hebron.  
Arba was the father of Anak (Josh 15:13; 21:11), and through Anak's sons – Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai, that is, Arba's grandsons – the Anakite lineage continued.  
Kiriath-Arba plays an important role already in the patriarchal narratives as the place where Sarah died and Abraham acquired the cave of Machpelah as a burial site.  
During the Israelites' conquest of Canaan, Caleb received the city as his inheritance and drove out Anak's descendants, thus bringing Arba's long-standing influence over the Hebron area to an end.

versions.summary: Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim, a people of giants who lived in the land of Canaan. The city Kiriath-Arba (later known as Hebron) was named after him. He is regarded as the ancestor of Anak, and his descendants, the Anakim, were feared for their enormous size.
versions.title: The Greatest Among the Anakim
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'The greatest among the Anakim' is appropriate, but Joshua 14:15 describes him as 'the greatest man among the Anakim'. This could be clarified slightly for better clarity.; [major] The role 'warrior' is not supported by the Bible. Arba is primarily described as a patriarch/founder and the greatest among the Anakim. There is no biblical text that specifically calls him a warrior. The role should be changed to 'patriarch' and possibly 'founder of Kiriath-Arba'.; [minor] The summary is well formulated, but it should clarify that the relationship between Arba and Anak can be interpreted differently – some texts call Arba 'father of Anak' (Josh 15:13; 21:11), while others may be understood as meaning Arba was the foremost in Anak's lineage. The wording could be nuanced slightly.; [minor] The era 'patriarchs' is acceptable since Arba is linked to the time of the patriarchs through Gen 23:2 (Kiriath-Arba/Hebron). However, his exact lifespan is unknown and could also be placed in a broader pre-conquest period. Nevertheless, 'patriarchs' remains the best available option.; [minor] In the fourth key event (Caleb takes Kiriath-Arba), it states that Caleb drove out 'the three sons of Anak'. It is more precise to say these were three descendants/clans of Anak (Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai), as mentioned in the fifth event. The last two events overlap somewhat and could have been combined.; [major] Footnotes are missing. There are rich linguistic, archaeological and historical details connected to Arba, the Anakim, and Kiriath-Arba/Hebron that should be covered.

versions.summary: Arba was according to the Bible the greatest man among the Anakites, a people of giants who lived in the land of Canaan. The city Kirjath-Arba ('City of Arba'), which later became known as Hebron, was named after him. He is regarded as the father of Anak (Josh 15:13; 21:11), and his descendants – the Anakites – were feared for their enormous size. Arba is mentioned already in the patriarchal narratives, where Kirjath-Arba is the place where Sarah died and Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah as a burial site. His descendants were eventually driven out by Caleb during the Israelite conquest of Canaan.
versions.title: The greatest man among the Anakim
versions.reason: [minor] The phrasing "according to the Bible" is redundant in a biblical person profile – all content is by definition based on the Bible. It should be removed for a more direct and elegant formulation. Additionally, the text should differ sufficiently from the previous version.; [minor] The sentence about Sarah's death and Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah concerns Abraham more than Arba. It may be kept as context but should be toned down so that the focus remains on Arba.; [minor] In the keyEvent "Caleb takes Kirjath-Arba," Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai are mentioned as descendants of Arba through Anak. According to Joshua 15:14, they are "the three sons of Anak," that is, grandchildren of Arba. The phrasing "clans" is somewhat imprecise – they were individuals/sons of Anak.; [minor] Arba likely lived in an undefined time before the patriarchs or at the same time as them. "Patriarchs" is acceptable since his city is mentioned in the patriarchal narratives, but strictly speaking, he is a pre-patriarchal figure. Nevertheless, "patriarchs" is the closest alternative in the list.; [minor] Arba is described as "the greatest man among the Anakim" (Joshua 14:15), which suggests some kind of leadership role. "Leader" or "chief" could be considered as an additional role.

versions.reason: [minor] The role of 'chief among the Anakim' is a reasonable interpretation, but the Bible specifically describes him as 'the greatest man among the Anakim' without using a title like 'chief'. The role can be retained as a qualified interpretation, but it should be noted that this is an inference rather than an explicit biblical title.; [minor] In the fourth key event, Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai are mentioned as 'descendants of Arba'. Technically, they were sons of Anak, who in turn was the son of Arba – thus grandsons of Arba. The description 'descendants' is correct, but it can be clarified that they were his grandsons to avoid sounding like direct sons.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but the sentence about Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai as 'sons of Anak' can be clarified by noting that these were therefore Arba's grandsons, to make the family relationship clearer for the reader.

footnotes.text: The name 'Arba' (Hebrew: אַרְבַּע) means 'four' in Hebrew. It is debated whether this is a proper name or a title, and some rabbinic sources speculate that it may refer to four giants or four great men.

Kiriath-Arba (קִרְיַת אַרְבַּע) literally means 'Arba's city' or 'the city of the four.' The city later became known as Hebron and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. Archaeological excavations at Tell er-Rumeide have uncovered settlement walls from the Bronze Age that can be linked to the Canaanite period when the Anakim lived there.

The Anakim (Hebrew: עֲנָקִים) are described as a people of unusually large stature. They are mentioned both in the books of Moses and in Joshua, and may have been part of a broader tradition of giant peoples in the ancient Near East. Some scholars have connected them to the Egyptian Execration texts from the second millennium BCE, which mention rulers in Canaan with Semitic names.

In rabbinic tradition (including Bereshit Rabbah), the origin of the Anakim and their relationship to the Nephilim (Gen 6:4) is discussed. Some rabbinic commentators view Arba as the founder of a dynastic line of giants who dominated the Hebron region until the Israelite conquest.

Hebron plays a central role in the patriarchal narratives. Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah there (Gen 23), and the city later became Caleb's inheritance (Josh 14:13–14). The fact that the city originally bore Arba's name highlights the pre-Israelite settlement history of the area.

The Hebrew base text in Josh 14:15 describes Arba as 'ha-adam ha-gadol ba-anaqim' – 'the greatest man among the Anakim.' The word 'gadol' can mean both physically large and powerful/prominent, and it is debated whether it primarily refers to Arba's physical size or his status and influence.
